name: ターバンカレー 総本店 (Turban Curry Sohonten)

claims.text: Curry roux is wheat-flour based and the signature toppings are breaded/fried cutlets and croquettes, so wheat is pervasive throughout the kitchen.
Menu is centered on pork cutlet, sausage, hamburg steak and a meat-stock roux; no plant-based items are documented.
House sushi soy sauce is blended on a Kanazawa Ohno shoyu base; conventional Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.

name: わ食場 はす家 本店 (Wa Shokuba Hasuya Honten)

claims.text: Kaga cuisine such as jibuni is thickened with flour and seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce; no gluten-free handling is documented.
The menu is built on Japanese seasonings (soy sauce, dashi); standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. No wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
Dishes rely on fish/bonito dashi and the kitchen centers on seafood and meat, so plant-only dishes would likely still contact animal-based dashi.
Desserts are assembled in a small kitchen using wheat-based sponge and pastry cream, so flour is present and cross-contamination is likely; no gluten-free handling is documented.
The signature Mont Blanc and related sweets contain dairy (mascarpone, custard, fresh cream) and egg (meringue, sponge); no separate vegan preparation is documented.
The chestnut paste itself uses only Noto aged roasted chestnuts with no added sugar, so the chestnut element is naturally simple.

name: 焼肉ホルモンくろまる (Yakiniku Horumon Kuromaru)

claims.text: Yakiniku/horumon served on shared grills with soy-based house tare; no gluten-free accommodation or allergen handling is documented.
The restaurant's signature is its house-made tare (秘伝の特製ダレ), which in Japanese grill houses is virtually always soy-sauce-based and thus contains wheat.
An all-meat grill concept; the only plant item noted is a complimentary cabbage starter, and all cooking happens on grills shared with offal and meat.

name: 焼肉ホルモン 芝生 (Yakiniku Horumon Shibafu)

claims.text: Signature dishes center on house white and black sauces, the black being a sweet-savory miso preparation, and the meal ends with wheat finishing noodles — indicating soy/miso/wheat are integral and not avoidable.
Menu is entirely grilled beef and beef offal cooked on shared griddles; no plant-based offerings documented.
The official site notes that allergy information is available (linked on the site), so diners with allergies can request details.
An English menu and international reservation support are offered, easing communication about ingredients for non-Japanese diners.

This is a Kyoto-style izakaya whose signature dish is a wagyu offal hot pot (horumon nabe) built on a white-miso broth. Miso, broth seasonings, and izakaya cooking like this almost always involve wheat-containing ingredients and shared pots and surfaces, so it should not be considered celiac-safe. Confirm every ingredient directly with the kitchen before relying on it.
Dishes here lean on miso and typical Japanese seasonings; most Japanese soy sauce and miso-based broths contain wheat. Assume gluten is present unless staff confirm a specific wheat-free preparation.

The kitchen centers on wagyu and offal hot pot, and broths in this style are typically made with bonito/meat-based dashi. There is no documented dedicated vegan menu or separate-prep process, so vegan diners should confirm in advance what, if anything, can be made plant-based.

This is a traditional wheat-noodle ramen shop. The noodles are wheat-based and the signature soup is a soy-sauce broth, so a standard bowl is not gluten-free and is not safe for celiacs. No gluten-free option is documented.

Wheat noodles are cooked in shared boiling water and the soy-based soup is central to every bowl, so cross-contamination with wheat/gluten should be assumed throughout. No celiac-aware handling is documented; confirm directly with staff if you have celiac disease.
The soup is a soy-sauce (shoyu) base, and most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat. The broth itself should therefore be treated as containing gluten in addition to the wheat noodles.

This is a pork-soy ramen shop: the broth and the thick-cut braised chashu are pork-based, so there is no vegan option and animal products are present throughout the kitchen. The menu is essentially soy-sauce ramen only, with no documented vegetable-only dish.
